scenario: WIBTA for selling what I receive in my dad's will? | Obligatory "I'm on mobile, so sorry for mistakes." I (22M) have a very large family. Both of my parents have 3 kids from past relationships, and I'm the only child they have together. My dad (71) never divorced his previous wife, but has been with my mom (61) for the past 25 years. My dad is a severe alcoholic and has a bunch of other health problems. So the talk of his will has come up a few times. He owns the house we currently live in, his (separated) wife's house, and a bar that has 2 apartments above it. As of now, his wife's house would remain her's or if she passes, go to their 3 children. The house we live in now, would be split amongst the 4 of us. The bar and the apartments would go solely to me. My mom is worried she won't get anything when he does pass away, so she constantly asks if I'll give her half of the bar. I personally want nothing to do with the bar due it being a cause for my parent's alcoholism. My mom says I should just give it all to her if that's the case. I would ask her to at least buy out my half, but she has been mentally abusive to me for most of my life, and constantly sabotaged anything I've done to try and better my own life. I've recently thought about just selling my quarter of the house to my siblings, and the entire bar to them or anyone else who wants it. WIBTA if I decided to leave my mom out of anything I get from my dad's will?

Islamic Perspective on Inheritance (Waqf & Wills)** - **Inheritance (Faraid):** Islam mandates that assets be divided among heirs as per **Quranic rules (Surah An-Nisa 4:11-12)**. You, as the only child of your parents together, have a **specific share** in the inheritance of your father (and mother, if applicable). - **Wills (Wasiyyah):** A Muslim can leave up to **1/3 of their estate** in a will (Surah Al-Baqarah 2:185). However, this must not conflict with the mandatory shares of heirs. - **Selling Inheritance:** Islam does not prohibit selling inherited property, but it must be done **fairly and justly**, ensuring no one is wronged (especially heirs with legal rights). ### **2. Your Specific Situation** - **Your father’s will:** Since he owns multiple properties, his will can allocate assets (within legal limits) to specific people, but **mandatory heirs (like you and your siblings) still have rights**. - **Your mother’s claim:** She is not a mandatory heir in your father’s will (since she is not his wife in the Islamic sense—he was never divorced, but they lived separately). However, if she was his wife at the time of death (even if separated), she would have a **mandatory share** (1/8 if no children, but since you exist, it’s more complex). - **Your siblings’ rights:** Since you are the only child of both parents together, you and your siblings (from his first marriage) are **co-heirs** in the house and bar. You cannot unilaterally sell your share without their consent (unless they agree). ### **3. Your Proposed Action: Selling the Bar & House** - **Selling the bar:** If you sell it, the proceeds must be divided **fairly among all heirs** (you, your siblings, and possibly your mother if she has a claim). You cannot keep it all or give it to others without their consent. - **Selling your share in the house:** You can sell it, but the money must be divided among all co-owners (you, your siblings, and possibly your mother if she has a claim). - **Excluding your mother:** If she has a **legal claim** (e.g., if she was your father’s wife at death), excluding her would be **unjust and against Islamic principles**. If she was **not his wife** (e.g., if he was never divorced but lived separately), she may have no claim—but this is legally complex and requires clarification. ### **4. Emotional & Psychological Factors** - Your mother’s **mental abuse** and **sabotage** are serious issues, but **Islam does not condone retaliation in inheritance matters**. You must handle this with **justice, not vengeance**. - If she is **not a legal heir**, you can refuse to give her anything, but you must **prove her lack of claim** (e.g., through legal advice). - If she **does have a claim**, you must fulfill it, even if it’s difficult. ### **5. What Should You Do?** 1. **Consult a Muslim legal expert (Mufti/Islamic lawyer)** to clarify: - Was your mother your father’s wife at the time of death? - What are the exact inheritance shares of you, your siblings, and your mother? 2. **Do not sell the bar or house without agreement**—this could lead to legal disputes. 3. **If you want to avoid the bar**, you can: - **Sell your share** and distribute the money fairly. - **Give it to charity** (if you have no legal obligation to heirs). - **Use it for a legitimate purpose** (e.g., funding your education, helping siblings). 4. **Do not exclude your mother unfairly**—if she has no claim, that’s one thing, but if she does, you must fulfill it. ### **Final Verdict: Was It Right or Wrong?** - **If you exclude your mother without a valid Islamic/legal reason → Wrong (Zina’ in Islamic terms, as it’s unjust).** - **If you sell your share fairly and distribute proceeds to all heirs → Right.** - **If you give the bar to charity or a legitimate cause (after fulfilling heirs' rights) → Right.** - **If you keep it all for yourself or give it to others without consent → Wrong.** ### **Best Course of Action:** ✅ **Get legal clarity** on your mother’s status. ✅ **Distribute inheritance justly** (no favoritism, no exclusion of heirs). ✅ **Avoid emotional decisions**—let justice guide you. ✅ **If the bar causes harm**, sell it and use the money for good (charity, siblings, etc.).
